---
title: "Background & Related Work"
---

Work on drug shortages falls into three groups: government analyses that characterize the problem
and its causes, peer-reviewed attempts to predict shortages from operational data, and public
implementations that use FDA's own shortage feed. Each shapes this project differently.

## What Government Analyses Establish

**Shortages are an economic phenomenon, not primarily a manufacturing one.** FDA's Drug Shortages
Task Force examined 163 drugs that went into shortage between 2013 and 2017 and concluded that the
root causes are structural: there is little incentive to produce low-margin generic drugs, the
market does not reward manufacturers for mature quality systems, and contracting practices push
prices toward unsustainable levels [@fda2019roots]. The report's central insight for this project
is that shortage risk is predictable *in principle* because it is tied to observable market
characteristics — margin pressure, genericization, and quality history — rather than to random
manufacturing accidents.

**Specific, measurable factors correlate with shortage risk.** GAO found that shortages
concentrate in sterile injectables and older generic drugs, and are strongly associated with
identifiable market conditions rather than distributed evenly across the drug supply
[@gao2016factors]. This directly motivates RQ2: the attributes GAO identifies — dosage form,
generic status, market age — are all recoverable from the NDC Directory and Orange Book, which
makes them testable at scale.

**The problem is ongoing and the response remains reactive.** GAO's 2025 assessment found 102
active shortages as of July 2024 and noted that while the number of *new* shortages has generally
declined since 2020, shortages are lasting *longer* [@gao2025coordination]. It also found HHS
lacks a coordinating mechanism across its shortage activities. The persistence of the problem
despite a decade of policy attention is what makes advance warning valuable.

**Duration varies enormously by route of administration.** ASPE's analysis of 2018–2023 found 258
unique active ingredients in shortage, represented by 1,961 products, with median duration of 4.6
years for injectables versus 1.6 years for orals and 2.2 years for topicals [@aspe2025shortages].
Two things follow. First, it validates our choice of **ingredient &times; route** as the unit of
analysis — route is not a minor covariate, it is a primary axis of variation. Second, ASPE's
published survival medians give us an external benchmark to validate our reconstructed duration
estimates against.

## What the Prediction Literature Establishes

**Shortages are predictable from operational data, at moderate accuracy.** Pall et al. predicted
shortage severity one month ahead using Canadian pharmacy dispensing data, reaching roughly 69%
accuracy across four severity classes without any manufacturer or supplier inventory data
[@pall2023predicting]. Their most informative features were consumption-side: days of supply per
patient, total days of supply, and prior shortage history. This is important context for our
expectations — it suggests meaningful signal exists, while setting a realistic accuracy
expectation well short of near-perfect.

**Duration and cause are separately modelable.** Roe et al. built two models on 1,054
regulatory-reported South Korean shortage cases from 2018–2024: one estimating shortage duration
ranges (62% accuracy), one classifying cause into seven categories (>70% weighted F1)
[@roe2026korea]. Shortage incidence *frequency* — how often a drug has been short before — was
their most influential variable. Two lessons carry over: recurrence history is a strong feature
and we should construct it explicitly, and duration is a legitimate modeling target in its own
right, which supports our stated contingency framing.

**Neither study can be directly transferred.** Both rely on data we do not have. Pall et al. use
pharmacy dispensing records from a single health system; Roe et al. use a national regulatory
reporting system with mandatory cause attribution. In the US, no equivalent public dispensing
panel exists, and FDA's shortage file carries cause codes that are unnormalized and incomplete.
Our approach substitutes *supply-side* signals — product lifecycle records and approval data —
for the consumption-side data these studies depend on.

## Public Implementations Using FDA Data

Two public GitHub projects attempt roughly this task on FDA data.

`DengDuangLang111/Drug_Shortage_Prediction` [@dengduanglang2026] reconstructs history from 43
monthly Internet Archive snapshots (2019-10 to 2026-04), producing a 27,896-row medicine-month
panel and an 8,876-row training set with 60- and 90-day forward labels. This is close to our
framing and confirms the reconstruction approach is sound. Its scope limit is that it covers only
WHO Essential Medicines List molecules.

`Anirudh-Sohaney/medi-tracker` [@sohaney2026] provides an NDC9 &times; supplier &times; month panel of 254,316
rows spanning 2012–2026. It is useful as a cross-check, but it is a duration panel rather than a
balanced onset panel — `shortage_active = 1` on 252,886 of 254,316 rows — and its pre-2020 months
are backfilled rather than observed.

Neither is peer-reviewed; both are personal or student projects with no associated publication.

## The Gap This Project Addresses

Three gaps follow from the above.

**The historical record is destroyed by default, and most work inherits that limitation.** FDA
purges resolved shortages after roughly six months; as of September 2026 the live file retained 7
resolved records out of 1,634. Onset counts taken from the live file are severely length-biased.
We reconstruct 10,967 episodes across 1,416 drugs from 102 archived captures, of which 2,028 carry
resolution dates.

**Supply-side lifecycle data is unused.** FDA's NSDE file retains product records after delisting,
where the current NDC Directory drops them. This is not a minor convenience: historical shortage
records point at products that have since been delisted, so joining them to the live directory
discards more than half the data, and discards it *non-randomly* — biased toward exactly the
discontinued products a shortage model should care about. NSDE also enables a monthly count of
active package codes per ingredient &times; route going back to 2010, which is what makes RQ1's
leading-indicator question answerable at all. Neither prior implementation uses it.

**Coverage is narrower than the problem.** Prior public work restricts itself to WHO Essential
Medicines List molecules. We work over the full approved prescription universe (2,897 ingredient
&times; route units) which is both broader and, importantly, selected on criteria unrelated to
perceived importance.

Together these define the contribution: a shortage-onset analysis built on reconstructed labels
over the complete approved prescription universe, using supply-side product lifecycle signals that
existing work leaves on the table, and validated temporally with explicit controls against the
target leakage that makes this task look far easier than it is.
